strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical preference elicitation through natural language feedback
Sensible hybrid architecture that combines LLM strengths for language understanding with BO's principled uncertainty quantification and exploration
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ environments with systematic ablation studies examining design choices (pairwise vs scalar, pair selection, prior knowledge)
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines in feedback-limited regimes across diverse utility function types
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed pseudocode, complete prompts, and implementation details in appendices
Practical design considerations demonstrated, including domain prior incorporation that significantly improves performance
weaknesses: Critical circular reasoning: human feedback is simulated by an LLM containing ground-truth utility functions in prompts (Appendix B.3), making it unclear whether results transfer to real human preferences. This oracle-informed setup fundamentally undermines the main claims

Lack of real-world validation: paper mentions 'real-world optimization campaigns in online A/B testing' but provides zero details, results, or evidence. All experiments use LLM-simulated oracle-informed feedback

Limited technical novelty: individual components (BO, preference learning, LLM few-shot learning) are well-established. Prior work exists on LLM + BO combinations (Liu et al. 2024, Austin et al. 2024). Contribution is primarily engineering-focused

Fading advantage in longer horizons: Figure 3 shows LILO's benefits diminish significantly by iteration 8, with baselines largely catching up, suggesting the natural language advantage applies only to early feedback-limited phases

Insufficient LLM reliability analysis: while using 5 samples per comparison, no investigation of consistency rates, failure modes, or systematic biases. Acknowledged fidelity limitations not deeply explored
Missing scalability analysis: no computational cost analysis despite requiring multiple LLM calls per pair per iteration. Practical deployment concerns unaddressed
No theoretical foundation: lacks convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or theoretical characterization of when the hybrid approach is beneficial
Design choice justification limited: multiple decisions (K=64 pairs, 5 LLM samples, specific prompts) appear somewhat arbitrary with insufficient principled justification

Assumption of preference consistency unrealistic: framework assumes consistent utility function but real humans exhibit preference reversals and context-dependent preferences; no robustness analysis provided
Cold-start initialization: DM's first message hard-coded in experiments, making true cold-start performance assessment impossible and reducing practical applicability

Experimental limitations: quantitative baselines receive ground-truth feedback while LILO receives LLM-simulated feedback (asymmetric setup), only 4 outcome functions tested, no formal statistical significance tests, no human user studies

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem combining natural language feedback with Bayesian optimization through a principled hybrid approach that preserves BO's calibrated uncertainty
Demonstrates natural language feedback is information-dense (~8-16 pairwise comparisons per NL statement), with comprehensive experiments across 10 diverse environments

Comprehensive experimental validation with proper baselines (LLM-only methods, quantitative feedback methods), 32 replications, and extensive ablations covering feedback batch size, prior knowledge, acquisition functions, and LLM choice
Technically sound integration of LLM preference interpretation with pairwise GP modeling and qEUBO acquisition; validates pairwise labeling outperforms direct utility scoring
Extensible to high-dimensional unstructured outcomes (text summarization) without explicit outcome space modeling; includes textual prior knowledge incorporation for warm-starting
Excellent reproducibility with all prompts provided, detailed algorithms, implementation details, and promised code release; clear writing with effective problem formulation
weaknesses: Critical limitation: all experiments use LLM-simulated decision makers, not real humans; unclear how LILO handles real human feedback inconsistency, cognitive biases, and non-transitivity—severely limits practical applicability claims

LILO's advantage diminishes substantially over longer horizons (Figure 14), with quantitative baselines matching/exceeding LILO by trial 16; main experiments (T=8) are in the regime where LILO excels but may not reflect realistic budget-limited settings

Limited theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, regret bounds, or formal treatment of how LLM label noise (85-90% accuracy from Figure 13) propagates through optimization; unclear whether pairwise GP adequately handles this noise

Heavy dependence on LLM quality and consistency not thoroughly investigated: same LLM used for both LILO and simulated DM introduces correlation; only 3 LLM variants tested; no analysis of robustness to systematic LLM biases
Posterior calibration unclear under label noise: with 85-90% LLM accuracy, uncertainty estimates may not reflect true model uncertainty; no validation that GP posterior remains meaningful/calibrated

Incomplete practical guidance: LLM API costs not discussed; labeling budget K and chunk size S sensitivity not explored; scalability in high-dimensional parameter/outcome spaces unclear; initialization sensitivity (Figure 12) shows strong dependence on prior quality but limited analysis
